claim: Gokushoviruses are single-stranded, circular DNA bacteriophages found in metagenomic datasets from diverse ecosystems worldwide, including human gut microbiomes.
source: Gokushoviruses are single-stranded, circular DNA bacteriophages found in metagenomic datasets from diverse ecosystems worldwide, including human gut microbiomes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Isolates of gokushoviruses are exceedingly rare, known only from three obligate intracellular bacterial genera.
source: Isolates are exceedingly rare, known only from three obligate intracellular bacterial genera.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work on Spiroplasma, Chlamydia, and Bdellovibrio hosts.

claim: Gokushovirus virions can reliably infect and lysogenize hosts by hijacking a conserved chromosome-dimer resolution system.
source: We demonstrate that virions can reliably infect and lysogenize hosts by hijacking a conserved chromosome-dimer resolution system.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data presented in the manuscript, including integration assays and genetic complementation experiments.

claim: Sequence motifs required for lysogeny are detectable in other metagenomically defined gokushoviruses.
source: Sequence motifs required for lysogeny are detectable in other metagenomically defined gokushoviruses
evidence: This is supported by the bioinformatic analysis of dif-motifs across gokushovirus MAGs presented in the manuscript.

claim: Even partial motifs enable phages to persist cytoplasmically without leading to collapse of their host culture.
source: we show that even partial motifs enable phages to persist cytoplasmically without leading to collapse of their host culture.
evidence: This is demonstrated through serial transfer experiments with phages lacking complete dif-motifs.

claim: The ability to employ multiple, disparate survival strategies is likely key to the long-term persistence and global distribution of Gokushovirinae.
source: This ability to employ multiple, disparate survival strategies is likely key to the long-term persistence and global distribution of Gokushovirinae.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and ecological observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Single-stranded circular DNA (ssDNA) phages of the family Microviridae are among the most common and rapidly evolving viruses present in the human gut.
source: Single-stranded circular DNA (ssDNA) phages of the family Microviridae are among the most common and rapidly evolving viruses present in the human gut (Lim et al., 2015; Minot et al., 2013; Manrique et al., 2017; Shkoporov et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Members of the subfamily Gokushovirinae are detected in metagenomic datasets from diverse environments, ranging from methane seeps to stromatolites, termite hindguts, freshwater bogs and the open ocean.
source: Within the Microviridae, members of the subfamily Gokushovirinae are detected in metagenomic datasets from diverse environments, ranging from methane seeps to stromatolites, termite hindguts, freshwater bogs and the open ocean (Bryson et al., 2015; Desnues et al., 2008; Quaiser et al., 2015; Tikhe and Husseneder, 2018; Tucker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous metagenomic studies.

claim: Full assembly of gokushovirus phages from metagenomic data is easy due to their small, circular genomes.
source: Due to their small, circular genomes, full assembly of these phages from metagenomic data is easy (Creasy et al., 2018; Labonté and Suttle, 2013; Roux et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on metagenomic assembly of microviruses.

claim: More than a thousand complete metagenome-assembled microvirus genomes have been deposited to NCBI as of beginning of 2020.
source: more than a thousand complete metagenome-assembled microvirus genomes have been deposited to NCBI as of beginning of 2020.
evidence: This is a factual statement about database contents at a specific time point.

claim: Microviridae have been isolated from very few hosts, hardly representative of their diversity as a whole.
source: In contrast, Microviridae have been isolated from very few hosts, hardly representative of their diversity as a whole
evidence: This is supported by the limited number of isolated microviruses cited in the manuscript.

claim: The only readily cultivable member of the Microviridae family is phiX174, which is classified to the distantly related subfamily Bullavirinae.
source: the only readily cultivable member of this family is phiX174, which is classified to the distantly related subfamily Bullavirinae (Doore and Fane, 2016; Krupovic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on phiX174 and microvirus taxonomy.

claim: PhiX and phiX-like phages are rare in nature and occupy a small specialist niche as lytic predators of select strains of Escherichia coli.
source: While phiX and phiX-like phages are among the most well-studied groups of viruses, they are rare in nature and occupy a small specialist niche as lytic predators of select strains of Escherichia coli (Michel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on phiX ecology.

claim: The Gokushovirinae and several other subfamilies of Microviridae are seemingly abundant in the environment but almost exclusively known from metagenomic datasets.
source: Conversely, the Gokushovirinae and several other (though not formally described) subfamilies of Microviridae are seemingly abundant in the environment but almost exclusively known from metagenomic datasets (Creasy et al., 2018; Székely and Breitbart, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous metagenomic studies.

claim: Estimates of gokushovirus numbers could be biased due to the methods used to prepare metagenomic samples.
source: although estimates of their actual numbers could be biased due to the methods used to prepare metagenomic samples (Kim and Bae, 2011; Roux et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on metagenomic methodology.

claim: The only isolated gokushoviruses are lytic parasites recovered from the host-restricted intracellular bacteria Spiroplasma, Chlamydia and Bdellovibrio.
source: Despite their apparent prevalence in the environment, the only isolated gokushoviruses are lytic parasites recovered from the host-restricted intracellular bacteria Spiroplasma, Chlamydia and Bdellovibrio (Brentlinger et al., 2002; Garner et al., 2004; Ricard et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original isolation papers for these phages.

claim: It seems unlikely that Gokushovirinae only infect intracellular bacteria given their regular occurrence in metagenomes from diverse habitats.
source: Given their regular occurrence in metagenomes from diverse habitats, it seems unlikely that Gokushovirinae only infect intracellular bacteria, and their lack of recovery from other hosts is puzzling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ecological distribution of gokushoviruses.

claim: Typical gokushoviruses pack their 4000-6000 nt genomes, composed of 3–11 genes, into tailless icosahedral phage capsids.
source: Typical gokushoviruses pack their 4000-6000 nt genomes, composed of 3–11 genes, into tailless icosahedral phage capsids (Roux et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work characterizing gokushovirus genomes.

claim: No gokushoviruses encode an integrase, which has led to the assumption that they are lytic phages.
source: No gokushoviruses encode an integrase, which has led to the assumption that they are lytic phages.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of gokushoviruses and established knowledge about integrase function.

claim: The presence of prophages belonging to several undescribed groups of microviruses within the genomes of some Bacteroidetes and Alphaproteobacteria raises the possibility that some can be integrated through the use of host-proteins.
source: However, the presence of prophages belonging to several undescribed groups of microviruses within the genomes of some Bacteroidetes and Alphaproteobacteria (Krupovic and Forterre, 2011; Zhan and Chen, 2019; Zheng et al., 2018) raises the possibility that some can be integrated through the use of host-proteins, in a similar manner to the XerC/XerD dependent integration of ssDNA Inoviridae (Krupovic and Forterre, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on microvirus prophages and inovirus integration.

claim: All gokushovirus genomes assembled from metagenomic data lack multiple genes that are present in phiX-like phages.
source: All gokushovirus genomes assembled from metagenomic data lack multiple genes that are present in phiX-like phages (Roux et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous comparative genomic work.

claim: Gokushoviruses lack a peptidoglycan synthesis inhibitor that leads to host cell lysis, although some phages appear to have horizontally acquired bacterial peptidases.
source: Markedly absent are: (i) a peptidoglycan synthesis inhibitor that leads to host cell lysis (although some phages appear to have horizontally acquired bacterial peptidases)
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and comparison with phiX.

claim: Gokushoviruses lack a major spike protein involved in host cell attachment.
source: (ii) a major spike protein involved in host cell attachment (Doore and Fane, 2016; Roux et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on gokushovirus and phiX genomics.

claim: The absence of peptidoglycan synthesis inhibitor and major spike protein from gokushoviruses indicates that these phages might operate quite differently from phiX on a molecular level.
source: These proteins represent crucial elements in the infectious cycle of phiX, and their absence from other gokushoviruses indicates that these phages might operate quite differently on a molecular level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic differences between gokushoviruses and phiX.

claim: A large number of gokushovirus prophages are integrated into the genomes of enterobacteria.
source: Here we detect a large number of gokushovirus prophages integrated into the genomes of enterobacteria, contrasting with their predicted exclusively lytic lifestyle.
evidence: This is supported by the bioinformatic analysis presented in the Results section.

claim: Through transformation of a synthesized prophage genome into a laboratory strain of Escherichia coli, a novel gokushovirus capable of lysogenizing enterobacteria was cultivated.
source: Through transformation of a synthesized prophage genome into a laboratory strain of Escherichia coli, we cultivate a novel gokushovirus capable of lysogenizing enterobacteria.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the experimental work described in the Results section.

claim: The gokushovirus EC6098 is capable of passive integration via XerC/XerD mediated recombination of phage encoded dif-motifs with their bacterial counterparts.
source: Using this experimental model system, we demonstrate that this phage is capable of passive integration via XerC/XerD mediated recombination of phage encoded dif-motifs with their bacterial counterparts.
evidence: This is demonstrated through genetic complementation and mutant analysis experiments.

claim: The capability for XerC/XerD-mediated integration has evolved independently in multiple lineages of gokushoviruses.
source: We also show that this capability has evolved independently in multiple lineages of gokushoviruses
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of dif-motifs across gokushovirus lineages.

claim: There exists an intermediate, pseudolysogenic step between lytic and lysogenic lifestyle in gokushoviruses.
source: and demonstrate the existence of an intermediate, pseudolysogenic step between lytic and lysogenic lifestyle
evidence: This is demonstrated through serial transfer experiments with phages lacking complete integration machinery.

claim: Gokushoviruses can lead a decidedly different existence from that of previously characterized members of the Gokushovirinae.
source: indicating that gokushoviruses can lead a decidedly different existence from that of previously characterized members of the Gokushovirinae.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings showing lysogenic and pseudolysogenic capabilities.

claim: Querying fully assembled bacterial genomes with the major capsid protein VP1 of gokushovirus Chlamydia-phage 4 returned 95 high-confidence hits within the Enterobacteriaceae.
source: Querying fully assembled bacterial genomes with the major capsid protein VP1 of gokushovirus Chlamydia-phage 4 (NCBI Gene ID 3703676) returned 95 high-confidence hits (E-value <0.0001) within the Enterobacteriaceae (91 from Escherichia, and one each from Enterobacter, Salmonella, Citrobacter and Kosakonia; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the bioinformatic analysis performed in the study.

claim: Inspection of genomic regions revealed the presence of integrated prophages 4300–4700 bp in length with a conserved six-gene arrangement: VP4, VP5, VP3, VP1, VP2 and VP8.
source: Although Gokushovirinae were previously known only as lytic phages, inspection of each of the associated genomic regions revealed the presence of integrated prophages 4300–4700 bp in length and having a conserved six-gene arrangement: VP4 (replication initiation protein), VP5 (switch from dsDNA to ssDNA replication protein), VP3 (scaffold protein), VP1 (major capsid protein), VP2 (minor capsid protein) and VP8 (putative DNA-binding protein).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of the detected prophages.

claim: Most of the variation in genome size and sequence of enterogokushovirus prophages is confined to three regions: near the C-terminus of VP2, in the non-coding region between VP8 and VP2, and within VP1.
source: Most of the variation in both the genome size and sequence of these prophages is confined to three regions: (i) near the C-terminus of VP2, (ii) in the non-coding region between VP8 and VP2, and (iii) within VP1, whose hypervariability is characteristic of the Gokushovirinae (Chipman et al., 1998; Diemer and Stedman, 2016; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and analysis, with reference to Figure 1A and citations to previous work.

claim: All detected prophages are flanked by dif-motifs, which are 28 bp palindromic sites that are known to be the targets of passive integration by phages and other mobile elements.
source: All detected prophages are flanked by dif-motifs, which are 28 bp palindromic sites that are known to be the targets of passive integration by phages and other mobile elements (Blakely et al., 1993; Das et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by citations to previous work on dif-motifs.

claim: The dif-motifs upstream of the insertions are highly conserved and individually differ by, at most, one nucleotide from the canonical dif-motif of Escherichia coli.
source: The dif-motifs upstream of the insertions are highly conserved and individually differ by, at most, one nucleotide from the canonical dif-motif of Escherichia coli.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment and comparison of the detected dif-motifs.

claim: The upstream dif-motifs consist of a central 6 bp spacer flanked by two 11 bp arms, which bind tyrosine recombinases XerC/XerD during chromosome segregation and integration of mobile elements.
source: These upstream dif-motifs consist of a central 6 bp spacer flanked by two 11 bp arms, previously been shown to bind tyrosine recombinases XerC/XerD during chromosome segregation and integration of mobile elements (Castillo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by a citation to previous work on XerC/XerD binding.

claim: The dif-motifs downstream of detected prophages are more variable, particularly in the spacer region and XerD-binding arms, representing the phage dif-motifs integrated along with the phage.
source: In contrast, the dif-motifs downstream of detected prophages are more variable, particularly in the spacer region and XerD-binding arms, representing the phage dif-motifs integrated along with the phage (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A whole genome phylogeny of gokushovirus prophages shows a number of well-differentiated lineages, forming clades A-J that each contains members with >95% average nucleotide identity, and 14 singleton lineages with no close relatives.
source: A whole genome phylogeny of gokushovirus prophages shows a number of well-differentiated (bootstrap support 70% or higher) lineages, forming clades A-J that each contains members with >95% average nucleotide identity, and 14 singleton lineages with no close relatives (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prophages belonging to clade A-D are found dispersed across the host phylogeny, while prophage clade I is confined to a single E. coli clade.
source: For example, whereas prophages belonging to clade A-D are found dispersed across the host phylogeny, prophage clade I is confined to a single E. coli clade (possibly as a result of the limited number of detected prophages).
evidence: This is based on comparison of phage and host phylogenies shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In all but one case, each E. coli host harbors only a single gokushovirus prophage.
source: In all but one case, each E. coli host harbors only a single gokushovirus prophage.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the detected prophages in bacterial genomes.

claim: There is no obvious association between the presence of gokushovirus prophages and particular E. coli O-serotypes among those strains for which information on O-antigens is available.
source: Although phage attachment and infection sometimes depend on O-antigenicity, there is no obvious association between the presence of gokushovirus prophages and particular E. coli O-serotypes among those strains for which information on O-antigens is available (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on analysis of O-serotype data for strains harboring prophages.

claim: Four identical prophages belonging to clade C were detected in E. coli strains MOD1-EC5200 (O76:H19), MOD1-EC5181 (O132:H8), NCTC9043 (O43:H2) and MOD1-EC6266 (O124:H21).
source: For example, four identical prophages belonging to clade C could be detected in E. coli strains MOD1-EC5200 (O76:H19), MOD1-EC5181 (O132:H8), NCTC9043 (O43:H2) and MOD1-EC6266 (O124:H21) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and O-serotype data.

claim: Most gokushovirus prophages were detected in diverse E. coli strains isolated from various animals, mainly cattle and marmots.
source: Most gokushovirus prophages were detected in diverse E. coli strains isolated from various animals, mainly cattle and marmots, but five prophages were detected in isolates from humans, including one from a urinary tract infection (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on metadata associated with the bacterial strains harboring prophages.

claim: Five prophages were detected in isolates from humans, including one from a urinary tract infection.
source: but five prophages were detected in isolates from humans, including one from a urinary tract infection (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on metadata associated with the bacterial strains harboring prophages.

claim: Enterobacterial prophages form a well-supported, monophyletic clade within the Gokushovirinae.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of available gokushovirus genomes based on an alignment of the conserved VP1 and VP4 proteins (n = 855; including the enterobacterial prophages discovered in this study, the previously sequenced lytic gokushoviruses from Chlamydia, Spiroplasma and Bdellovibrio, and the metagenomically assembled gokushovirus genomes available from NCBI) returned enterobacterial prophages as a well-supported (97% bootstrap support), monophyletic clade within the Gokushovirinae (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The distinctiveness of the enterobacterial prophage clade, whose members share a conserved gene order and display an average nucleotide identity of >50%, advocates the formation of a new proposed genus within the family Microviridae (subfamily Gokushovirinae), named Enterogokushovirus.
source: The distinctiveness of this clade, whose members share a conserved (but not unique) gene order and display an average nucleotide identity of >50% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2), advocates the formation of a new proposed genus within the family Microviridae (subfamily Gokushovirinae), for which we suggest the name Enterogokushovirus on account of a distribution limited to members of the Enterobactericeae.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and genomic analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A unique feature of enterogokushoviruses among the Gokushovirinae appears to be the ability to exist as lysogens.
source: Since a unique feature of enterogokushoviruses among the Gokushovirinae appears to be the ability to exist as lysogens, we searched all other gokushovirus MAGs in our dataset for dif-like sequence motifs that might be indicative of lysogenic ability.
evidence: This is based on the detection of integrated prophages and comparison with other gokushoviruses.

claim: Similar dif-like motifs were detected in 48 genomes distributed sporadically throughout the gokushovirus phylogeny.
source: We detected similar motifs in 48 genomes distributed sporadically throughout the gokushovirus phylogeny.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic search for dif-motifs in gokushovirus MAGs.

claim: Aside from the enterogokushoviruses, there are two larger clades in which multiple genomes contain a dif-motif, with the rest of dif-bearing MAGs found largely as singletons.
source: Aside from the enterogokushoviruses, there are two larger clades in which multiple genomes contain a dif-motif, with the rest of dif-bearing MAGs found largely as singletons (Figure 2; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and dif-motif detection, shown in Figure 2.

claim: The majority of putative dif-motifs occurs in non-coding regions, and those detected within coding regions were typically at the 5'- or 3'-end of a predicted gene.
source: The majority of these putative dif-motifs occurs in non-coding regions, and those detected within coding regions were typically at the 5'- or 3'-end of a predicted gene, with a nearby alternative start or stop codon that could preserve the genetic integrity of the phage through integration and excision.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the genomic context of detected dif-motifs.

claim: The overall dearth of dif-like sequences in gokushoviruses sampled from diverse geographic and ecological settings highlights the distinctiveness of Enterogokushovirus genomes and lifestyle.
source: The overall dearth of dif-like sequences in gokushoviruses sampled from diverse geographic and ecological settings highlights the distinctiveness of Enterogokushovirus genomes and lifestyle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative analysis of dif-motif distribution.

claim: Only two integrated prophages corresponding to E. coli gokushoviruses were fully assembled from 1839 samples from eight metagenomic studies of human and cattle gut microbiomes.
source: We further attempted to determine the prevalence of enterobacterial gokushoviruses by interrogating 1839 samples from eight metagenomic studies of human and cattle gut microbiomes for the presence of closely related prophages. From these data, we were able to fully assemble only two integrated prophages corresponding to E. coli gokushoviruses, one from the fecal metagenome of an Austrian adult (0,05% of all reads in ERR688616) and the other from a Danish infant (0,02% of all reads in ERR525761) (see also Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on metagenomic assembly from multiple datasets.

claim: The integrity of prophage structure in all enterobacteria and the lack of premature stop codons suggested that these sequences represent intact, functional insertions into bacterial hosts.
source: The integrity of prophage structure in all enterobacteria and the lack of premature stop codons suggested that these sequences represent intact, functional insertions into bacterial hosts.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of the detected prophages.

claim: Sequences corresponding to prophages from four Escherichia strains were amplified, circularized and transformed into E. coli DH5α.
source: To confirm the functionality of Escherichia gokushovirus prophages, characterize their biology and provide a type strain, we attempted to construct phages from genomic DNA of Escherichia strains MOD1-EC2703, MOD1-EC5150, MOD1-EC6098 and MOD1-EC6163, selected to represent the diversity of gokushovirus prophages and hosts (Figure 1B). Sequences corresponding to prophages from these four Escherichia strains were amplified, circularized and transformed into E. coli DH5α (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure performed, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Supernatants from the transformed DH5α culture resulted in plaques for only one of four reconstructed phage genomes (EC6098) when used in agar-overlay assays with E. coli K12 BW25113 hosts.
source: Supernatants from the transformed DH5α culture were used in agar-overlay assays with E. coli K12 BW25113 hosts, resulting in plaques for only one of four reconstructed phage genomes (EC6098, derived from E. marmotae strain MOD1-EC6098 and belonging to prophage clade E (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental result shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DH5α alone did not produce plaques on BW25113 and vice versa.
source: While both DH5α and BW25113 possess other prophages which could produce false positives when screening for gokushovirus production (Chen et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2010), DH5α alone did not produce plaques on BW25113 and vice versa (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a control experiment result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Circularized gokushovirus genomes were detected in all four strains (MOD1-EC2703, MOD1-EC5150, MOD1-EC6098 and MOD1-EC6163) via PCR, but only MOD1-EC6098 produced plaques.
source: To corroborate the synthesis of EC6098 phages (and the inability to produce phages from the other three sequences), we additionally grew live cultures of MOD1-EC2703, MOD1-EC5150, MOD1-EC6098 and MOD1-EC6163 and via PCR detected the presence of circularized gokushovirus genomes in all four, but only MOD1-EC6098 produced plaques resembling those derived from synthetic EC6098 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Electron microscopic observation of pure EC6098 lysates revealed tailless icosahedral virions, 25–30 µm in size and displaying protrusions previously observed in other Gokushovirinae.
source: Electron microscopic observation of pure EC6098 lysates recovered at a buoyant density of around 1.3 g/cm−3 in CsCl gradients (the range expected for members of the Microviridae, Thurber et al., 2009), revealed tailless icosahedral virions, 25–30 µm in size and displaying protrusions previously observed in other Gokushovirinae (Chipman et al., 1998; Diemer and Stedman, 2016; Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3D,E and supported by citations.

claim: EC6098 represents the first isolation of a gokushovirus able to infect free-living bacteria as well as being able to integrate as a lysogen into bacterial genomes.
source: Because Gokushovirinae have only been recovered as lytic particles from intracellular bacteria, this represents the first isolation of a gokushovirus able to infect free-living bacteria as well as being able to integrate as a lysogen into bacterial genomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and comparison with previously known gokushoviruses.

claim: The presence of circularized phage genomes could readily be detected from surviving colonies in confluent plaques derived from agar-overlay assays.
source: We next investigated the process by which gokushoviruses integrate into the bacterial host chromosome (Figure 4A). The presence of circularized phage genomes could readily be detected from surviving colonies in confluent plaques derived from agar-overlay assays (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Using primers that flank both sides of the dif-motif in host strain BW25113, products were recovered that were enlarged by the length of the phage relative to colonies lacking the prophage.
source: Using primers that flank both sides of the dif-motif in host strain BW25113, we recovered products that were enlarged by the length of the phage relative to colonies lacking the prophage (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4A,C.

claim: Sequencing confirmed that phage EC6098 integrates downstream of the BW25113 dif-motif, which remains unchanged.
source: Sequencing confirmed that, in accordance with the integration site of detected prophages, phage EC6098 integrates downstream of the BW25113 dif-motif, which remains unchanged (corresponding to position 3,046,436–3,046,463 in the closed genome with accession number CP009273).
evidence: This is based on sequencing data confirming the integration site.

claim: Neither ΔxerC nor ΔxerD mutants of E. coli host strain BW25113 resulted in integration.
source: Because none of the gokushovirus prophages encodes an integrase, we predicted that host factors XerC and XerD might be responsible for prophage integration, similar to what has been hypothesized for microvirus-prophages in Bacteroidetes (Krupovic and Forterre, 2011). Neither ΔxerC nor ΔxerD mutants of E. coli host strain BW25113 resulted in integration
evidence: This is an experimental result from infection assays with knockout mutants.

claim: The ΔxerC mutant was restored by complementation with a plasmid expressing the intact version of xerC.
source: but the ΔxerC mutant was restored by complementation with a plasmid expressing the intact version of xerC.
evidence: This is an experimental result from complementation assays.

claim: Phages with incomplete or no dif-motifs successfully infected hosts but failed to integrate into host genomes.
source: Similarly, phages with incomplete (i.e., lacking either their XerC or XerD binding site within the dif-motif, termed here ΔdifC and ΔdifD) or no dif-motifs (ΔdifCD) successfully infected hosts (as evidenced by the presence of circularized phage genomes in host colonies that had survived infection), but failed to integrate into host genomes, demonstrating the need for cooperative XerC/XerD binding for successful lysogeny (Table 1, Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Table 1, Figure 4B,C.

claim: The retention of dif-motifs after integration indicates that the integration process is reversible.
source: However, the retention of dif-motifs after integration indicates that this process is reversible
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic structure of integrated prophages.

claim: There is a smaller fragment in addition to that indicating prophage insertion, corresponding to those cells in the same colony that do not harbor the integrated prophage.
source: As evident in Figure 4C, there is a smaller fragment, in addition to that indicating prophage insertion, that corresponds to those cells in the same colony that do not harbor the integrated prophage.
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: These cells persisted even after multiple rounds of re-streaking, and the median ratio of lysogens to non-lysogenic cells derived from clonal colonies approaches 4:1.
source: These cells persisted even after multiple rounds of re-streaking, and the median ratio of lysogens to non-lysogenic cells derived from clonal colonies approaches 4:1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Even in pure cultures, phages are continuously being excised and reintegrated, presumably as a result of XerC/XerD activity.
source: Even in pure cultures, phages are thus continuously being excised and reintegrated, presumably as a result of XerC/XerD activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of mixed lysogenic/non-lysogenic populations.

claim: Almost all bacterial colonies that survived infections, regardless of whether they were lysogenized or not, were found to contain circular phage DNA.
source: The removal of host factors xerC or xerD, the presence an incomplete phage dif-motif, or the lack of a dif-motif (as observed in the majority of Gokushovirinae) all prevent integration of phages into host genomes (Table 1, Figure 4C). However, almost all bacterial colonies that survived infections, regardless of whether they were lysogenized or not, were found to contain circular phage DNA (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The presence of circular phage DNA alone, regardless of integration into the host genome, conferred superinfection immunity.
source: and the presence of circular phage DNA alone, regardless of integration into the host genome, conferred superinfection immunity (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cultures in which phage DNA could only be detected in circularized form were capable of producing infectious particles at levels significantly higher than those of cultures containing integrated prophages.
source: In addition, cultures in which phage DNA could only be detected in circularized form were capable of producing infectious particles at levels significantly higher than those of cultures containing integrated prophages (Figure 5B, Wilcoxon rank-sum test p<0.01).
evidence: This is an experimental result with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The absence of alternative integration sites was verified by inverse PCR.
source: The absence of alternative integration sites, as verified by inverse PCR, suggested that gokushoviruses might be able to persist in the host cytoplasm without integration into the host genome.
evidence: This is based on inverse PCR experiments.

claim: Gokushoviruses might be able to persist in the host cytoplasm without integration into the host genome.
source: The absence of alternative integration sites, as verified by inverse PCR, suggested that gokushoviruses might be able to persist in the host cytoplasm without integration into the host genome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: All lysogenic cultures produced phage particles throughout the course of serial transfer experiments.
source: To determine whether this persistence is a transient phenomenon that eventually leads to either the loss of phages or the collapse of bacterial cultures, we performed serial transfers (1:1000 dilution) with a variety of host-phage combinations over the course of a month. We enumerated plaque formation from culture supernatant on host strain BW25113ΔfhuA to avoid false positives from widespread contaminating dsDNA phages such as phi80 and SW-1, which unlike EC6098 require outer membrane receptor FhuA for successful infection (Rotman et al., 2012; Song et al., 2019). As expected, all lysogenic cultures (i.e., wild type cultures with integrated gokushovirus prophages) produced phage particles throughout the course of the experiments.
evidence: This is an experimental result from serial transfer experiments.

claim: A third of all cultures where gokushoviruses were initially present only in the cytoplasm retained phage production over the course of a month despite the lack of integration.
source: However, a third of all cultures where gokushoviruses were initially present only in the cytoplasm (due to deletions in the host integration machinery or phage integration site) retained phage production over the course of a month despite the lack of integration (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an experimental result shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Gokushoviruses do not exist solely as lytic particles but can also exist as (pseudo)lysogens, in a carrier state that continuously produces phage particles without integrating into the genome.
source: Cumulatively, these results indicate that gokushoviruses do not exist solely as lytic particles, as previously believed, but can also exist as (pseudo)lysogens, in a carrier state that continuously produces phage particles without integrating into the genome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results from serial transfer and integration experiments.

claim: The new proposed genus, Enterogokushovirus, offers new insights into the understanding of the ecologically widespread group of Gokushovirinae phages.
source: Through the analysis of whole genome sequences and metagenomic databases, we defined a unique genus of Gokushovirinae prophages and subsequently synthesized a viable gokushovirus capable of infecting and integrating into the genomes of enteric bacteria. Since Gokushovirinae were previously known as exclusively lytic predators of a few intracellular bacteria (King et al., 2011), the new proposed genus, Enterogokushovirus, offers new insights into our understanding of this ecologically widespread group of phages.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: By confirming the existence of Gokushovirinae prophages in free-living bacteria, a seeming paradox was resolved in which a diverse and widespread lineage within the Microviridae appeared to be confined to rare pathogenic and parasitic bacteria.
source: First, by confirming the existence of Gokushovirinae prophages in free-living bacteria, we resolved a seeming paradox in which a diverse and widespread lineage within the Microviridae appeared to be confined to rare pathogenic and parasitic bacteria, such as Chlamydia (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the discovery of enterogokushoviruses in free-living bacteria.

claim: By demonstrating the integration of a gokushovirus into the E. coli genome, it was shown that these phages employ survival strategies beyond the lytic infection of hosts.
source: Second, by demonstrating the integration of a gokushovirus into the E. coli genome, we show that these phages employ survival strategies beyond the lytic infection of hosts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental demonstration of lysogeny.

claim: Enterogokushoviruses appropriate a highly conserved bacterial chromosome concatemer-resolution system that enables their integration into host genomes via homologous recombination.
source: Experimental characterization of the enterogokushovirus EC6098 isolated from an environmental strain of E. marmotae showed that these phages possess a dif-like recognition motif that, together with the host-encoded recombinases XerC/XerD, is required for lysogeny. In this manner, enterogokushoviruses appropriate a highly conserved bacterial chromosome concatemer-resolution system that enables their integration into host genomes via homologous recombination (Castillo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results and supported by a citation.

claim: The exact mechanism of the integration process still remains to be elucidated.
source: The exact mechanism of this integration process still remains to be elucidated: some phages and mobile elements are known to have different requirements for the bacterial XerC and/or XerD proteins (Midonet and Barre, 2015), which is perhaps the reason why we could only successfully reconstitute xerC but not xerD knockouts.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study and cites relevant literature.

claim: Phages with only partial DNA-binding motifs exist in a condition in which circularized phage genomes are present in the cytoplasm and virions are continuously released from the host.
source: We also show that phages with only partial DNA-binding motifs exist in a condition in which circularized phage genomes are present in the cytoplasm and virions are continuously released from the host.
evidence: This is based on experimental results with mutant phages.

claim: This strategy is similar to the pseudolysogenic state observed in crAssphage and other bacteriophages.
source: While it should be noted that this could be a laboratory-induced phenomenon, this strategy is similar to the pseudolysogenic state observed in crAssphage (Shkoporov et al., 2018) and other bacteriophages (Siringan et al., 2014), and helps explain the persistence of microviruses in the human gut (Minot et al., 2013; Shkoporov et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison with previously described phenomena, supported by citations.

claim: The sporadic distribution of dif-motifs among other gokushoviruses indicates that the ability to lysogenize bacterial hosts has been independently gained and lost multiple times during the evolution of this taxon.
source: Despite an exhaustive sampling of gokushoviral diversity from metagenomic datasets, the occurrence of dif-positive gokushoviruses is rare outside of the enterogokushoviruses. However, the sporadic distribution of dif-motifs among other gokushoviruses indicates that the ability to lysogenize bacterial hosts has been independently gained and lost multiple times during the evolution of this taxon.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic distribution of dif-motifs.

claim: The exclusively lytic gokushoviruses of Chlamydia might once have been able to integrate into their hosts' genomes since extant Chlamydia genomes contain coding sequences similar to the gokushoviral replication initiation and minor capsid proteins.
source: For example, the exclusively lytic gokushoviruses of Chlamydia (Śliwa-Dominiak et al., 2013) might once have been able to integrate into their hosts' genomes since extant Chlamydia genomes contain coding sequences similar to the gokushoviral replication initiation and minor capsid proteins (Read et al., 2000; Rosenwald et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation based on genomic evidence and supported by citations.

claim: Lysogenic cultures produce a considerably lower number of phage particles than non-lysogenic cultures but are less prone to the loss of phage.
source: We observed that lysogenic cultures produce a considerably lower number of phage particles than non-lysogenic cultures but are less prone to the loss of phage, indicating that the lytic and lysogenic lifecycles confer different tradeoffs.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from phage production and serial transfer experiments.

claim: The lytic and lysogenic lifecycles confer different tradeoffs.
source: We observed that lysogenic cultures produce a considerably lower number of phage particles than non-lysogenic cultures but are less prone to the loss of phage, indicating that the lytic and lysogenic lifecycles confer different tradeoffs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: Lysogeny is a 'safe' strategy for phages in situations where hosts are scarce, with vertical inheritance preventing the dilution of phage particles in the absence of hosts.
source: It has long been suggested that lysogeny is a 'safe' strategy for phages in situations where hosts are scarce, with vertical inheritance preventing the dilution of phage particles in the absence of hosts (e.g., Berngruber et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established theory supported by a citation.

claim: Lysis is advantageous when host availability is high.
source: Meanwhile, lysis (and its more abundant production of phage particles) is advantageous when host availability is high.
evidence: This is established theory in phage biology.

claim: Lytic microviruses in the human gut have been predicted to infect Bacteroidetes and other dominant members of that community.
source: Lytic microviruses (i.e., those lacking dif-motifs) in the human gut have been predicted to infect Bacteroidetes and other dominant members of that community (Shkoporov et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The enterobacterial hosts of the gokushovirus prophages generally do not reach very high abundances in the gut microbiome, usually constituting less than 0.1% of the bacterial population.
source: However, the enterobacterial hosts of the gokushovirus prophages described in this study generally do not reach very high abundances in the gut microbiome, usually constituting less than 0.1% of the bacterial population (Human Microbiome Project Consortium, 2012), prompting the evolution of lysogeny.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the Human Microbiome Project data.

claim: The low abundance of enterobacterial hosts in the gut microbiome prompted the evolution of lysogeny in enterogokushoviruses.
source: However, the enterobacterial hosts of the gokushovirus prophages described in this study generally do not reach very high abundances in the gut microbiome, usually constituting less than 0.1% of the bacterial population (Human Microbiome Project Consortium, 2012), prompting the evolution of lysogeny.
evidence: This is an inference connecting host abundance to the evolution of lysogeny.

claim: The de novo evolution of the XerCD-binding motifs appears to be common due to the high mutation rate of ssDNA phages and an estimated substitution rate of 10−5/ nucleotides/day in the human gut.
source: Perhaps due to the high mutation rate of ssDNA phages, typically two orders of magnitude higher than in dsDNA phages (Sanjuán et al., 2010), and an estimated substitution rate of 10−5/ nucleotides/day in the human gut (Minot et al., 2013), the de novo evolution of the XerCD-binding motifs appears to be common, with similar systems existing in other families of phage and mobile-elements (Das et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous work on mutation rates and similar systems.

claim: It is surprising that enterogokushoviruses have not previously been identified in human metagenomes given the current depths of microbiome sampling and sequencing.
source: Given the current depths of microbiome sampling and sequencing, it is surprising that enterogokushoviruses have not previously been identified in human metagenomes.
evidence: This is an observation about the rarity of enterogokushoviruses in metagenomic data.

claim: Among the more than 100,000 sequenced enterobacterial genomes currently available, fewer than 100 gokushovirus prophages were detected.
source: Even among the more than 100,000 sequenced enterobacterial genomes that are currently available, we detected fewer than 100 gokushovirus prophages, and no gokushovirus prophages were detected in the sequenced genomes of other bacteria.
evidence: This is a summary of the bioinformatic search results.

claim: No gokushovirus prophages were detected in the sequenced genomes of bacteria other than enterobacteria.
source: and no gokushovirus prophages were detected in the sequenced genomes of other bacteria.
evidence: This is a result from the bioinformatic search.

claim: The rarity of gokushoviruses existing as prophages might result from the process by which they integrate into genomes.
source: This rarity of gokushoviruses existing as prophages might result from the process by which they integrate into genomes: although possession of dif-motifs provides a simple, passive integration system, they also facilitate prophage excision (and as a result, continuous production of phage particles) in the absence of external stressors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations of excision and reintegration.

claim: Possession of dif-motifs provides a simple, passive integration system but also facilitates prophage excision.
source: although possession of dif-motifs provides a simple, passive integration system, they also facilitate prophage excision (and as a result, continuous production of phage particles) in the absence of external stressors.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations and known properties of XerC/XerD systems.

claim: XerCD-mediated removal of genetic elements has attained application in molecular biology.
source: In fact, XerCD-mediated removal of genetic elements has attained application in molecular biology (Bloor and Cranenburgh, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The Vibrio cholerae phage CTX secures itself as a prophage by destroying the dif site upon insertion to prevent premature XerCD-mediated excision.
source: To prevent premature XerCD-mediated excision, the Vibrio cholerae phage CTX secures itself as a prophage by destroying the dif site upon insertion (Val et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on CTX phage.

claim: Vibrio prophages that retain their dif-motifs are only rarely detected.
source: whereas Vibrio prophages that retain their dif-motifs are only rarely detected (Das et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The abundance of gokushoviruses in the environment, as apparent from their regularity in metagenomic datasets, suggests that they are only transient residents of bacterial chromosomes and usually occur in pseudolysogenic or lytic states in the wild.
source: The abundance of gokushoviruses in the environment, as apparent from their regularity in metagenomic datasets, suggests that they are only transient residents of bacterial chromosomes and usually occur in pseudolysogenic or lytic states in the wild.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and metagenomic observations.

claim: The discovery of this group of phages offers several new directions for the study of the Microviridae.
source: The discovery of this group of phages offers several new directions for the study of the Microviridae.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the implications of the work.

claim: The presence of numerous and diverse gokushovirus prophages in a wide variety of E. coli strains makes it possible to elucidate aspects of gokushovirus biology in a comparative evolutionary framework.
source: First, the presence of numerous and diverse gokushovirus prophages in a wide variety of E. coli strains now makes it possible to elucidate aspects of gokushovirus biology in a comparative evolutionary framework.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions enabled by this work.

claim: Demonstrating that the host ranges of the Gokushovirinae extends beyond intracellular bacteria increases the likelihood that additional members of this prevalent group of phages will be isolated from appropriate hosts.
source: Furthermore, demonstrating that the host ranges of the Gokushovirinae extends beyond intracellular bacteria increases the likelihood that additional members of this prevalent group of phages will be isolated from appropriate hosts.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings for future isolation efforts.

claim: The amplification of entire ssDNA phage genomes and subsequent transformation into appropriate hosts can aid in the description of other Microviridae subfamilies.
source: Additionally, the amplification of entire ssDNA phage genomes and subsequent transformation into appropriate hosts, as conducted in this study and previously with de novo synthesized phiX (Smith et al., 2003) can aid in the description of other Microviridae subfamilies.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological contribution of the work, supported by a citation.

claim: The Alpavirinae have been detected as prophages of Bacteroidetes but so far remain without isolates and denied official recognition.
source: A promising target for this would be the Alpavirinae, which have been detected as prophages of Bacteroidetes but so far remain without isolates and denied official recognition (Roux et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work on Alpavirinae.

claim: The value of isolating enterogokushoviruses goes beyond their abundance in nature and provides a genetically manipulable model system that will further the understanding of this group as a whole.
source: In conclusion, the value of isolating enterogokushoviruses goes beyond their abundance in nature and provides a genetically manipulable model system that will further the understanding of this group as a whole (Shkoporov and Hill, 2019).
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the significance of the work, supported by a citation.

claim: EC6098 virions are 25–30 µm in size.
source: revealed tailless icosahedral virions, 25–30 µm in size
evidence: This is based on electron microscopy measurements.

source: Electron microscopic observation of pure EC6098 lysates recovered at a buoyant density of around 1.3 g/cm−3 in CsCl gradients (the range expected for members of the Microviridae, Thurber et al., 2009)

source: Integrated prophage genomes range from 4316 to 4692 bp in length
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1A and based on genomic analysis.

source: Sequencing confirmed that, in accordance with the integration site of detected prophages, phage EC6098 integrates downstream of the BW25113 dif-motif, which remains unchanged (corresponding to position 3,046,436–3,046,463 in the closed genome with accession number CP009273).
evidence: This is based on sequencing data confirming the integration site.

source: We enumerated plaque formation from culture supernatant on host strain BW25113ΔfhuA to avoid false positives from widespread contaminating dsDNA phages such as phi80 and SW-1, which unlike EC6098 require outer membrane receptor FhuA for successful infection (Rotman et al., 2012; Song et al., 2019).
